newsitem.title: MEXICO: Investors take Cetes option on Mexico note - source.
newsitem.headline: Investors take Cetes option on Mexico note - source.

text.p: Investors in Mexico's dual-rate note, coming due this Wednesday, have overwhelmingly chosen to take the option that pays an interest rate tied to Mexican treasury bills or Cetes, a senior Mexican government official said on Monday.
The one-year $1.5 billion note offered investors the option of taking an interest rate tied to the Cetes, or to LIBOR, and the option to be paid in U.S. dollars or in pesos.
About half the investors opted for payment in pesos, with the other half taking the U.S. dollar payment option, the official, who declined to be identified, told Reuters.
When asked if the government planned to renew the dual-rate note, the official said, "Not for the time being."
The note was originally to total $500 million, but strong demand last year helped bump up the amount to $1.5 billion. The bond was placed in the European markets.
The note offered to pay a rate based on the 28-day Cetes, less 600 basis points, or the 12-month LIBOR.
"It is obvious that everyone has chosen the Cetes amount," the official said.
The Cetes interest payout was set at a running average of the 28-day Cetes, which one private sector analyst estimated at about 31.0 percent. On Monday, the 12-month LIBOR was 5-11/16.
On the dollar or peso option, things were less clear.
"It is more or less 50-50 for pesos and dollars," the official said. "We are getting both in pesos and dollars."
The government has already placed a number of bond issues to cover the maturing note.
In August, the Mexican federal government placed a deutschemark bond worth about $675 million.
The following month it placed a yen-denominated issue worth about $640 million. Then in November the govenrment placed a lira note worth about $325 million.
Analysts said when the dual-rate note was first placed it formed an important part of Mexico's return to international capital markets.
But at the same time, the dual-rate note was was expensive short-term paper when the government's strategy is to place longer-term issues.

"This note was one of their first re-entries into the international capital markets after the crisis and it was the one of the catalysts to get things going again. But it was very expensive for the Mexican government," said MMS International analyst Sonia Stromeyer.
Lead manager for the issue was Chemical Investment Bank Limited.
